To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
N-ethylmale-imide, which blocks G-protein function, blocks DSI, a form of GABAergic transmission that is absent in hippocampus of rats treated with pertussis toxin.
DSI is blocked by N-ethylmale-imide (NEM) and that NEM also increases GABA transmission in hippocampus.
NEM blocks DSI of both spontaneous and evoked GABAA receptor mediated inhibition, that NEM enhances quantal GABAergic transmission, and that NEM does not block DSI by blocking Ca2+entry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of DSI, a form of presynaptic modulation of GABA transmission that may have relevance to the pathophysiology of epilepsy.
a novel form of inhibition that is regulated by a G-protein and that can be studied in a single cell before and after GTP-binding protein block.
a process that regulates synaptic, GABAR-mediated inhibition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NEM blocks DSI of s- and evoked IPSC by a mechanism that involves inhibition of G-protein function.
NEM, by blocking G-proteins and increasing GABA release, abolishes DSI and increases spontaneous IPSC frequency.
NEM blocks DSI by inhibiting the G-proteins that are responsible for DSI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DSI is mediated by a pertussis toxin sensitive G-protein and that NEM can be used to block DSI.
DSI is a G-protein mediated process that is associated with a decrease in GABA release.
DSI is mediated by pertussis toxin sensitive G-proteins and that the G-protein-mediated DSI mechanism may be involved in a negative feedback mechanism to regulate synaptic, GABA transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DSI process is mediated via a G-protein that is blocked by N-ethylmaleamide.
DSI is blocked by acute inhibition of G proteins, and this is consistent with the hypothesis that a G-protein mediates DSI.
